The United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) and its precursor, the
Common Country Assessment (CCA), are both products of the reform program initiated by
Secretary-General Kofi Annan in 1997 aimed at preparing the UN for the challenges of
the 21st century. The UNDAF is a planning framework for the development operations of
the UN at the country level. It identifies a set of common objectives and strategies
for cooperation, a program framework and proposals for follow-up, monitoring and
evaluation. The UNDAF is based on both the content and the teamwork process of the
CCA. Further, the UNDAF is a key tool for helping the UN fulfill its development
mandate: to ensure the protection and inclusion of the poorest and most vulnerable,
to guarantee the universality of access to basic social services and to the benefits
of development, and to secure social, political, and cultural rights for all.
We have been fortunate this past year. The CCA and UNDAF have been carried out
concurrently with key national planning exercises, including the Second Five-Year
Plan, the Poverty Reduction Strategy and Action Plan (PRSAP) and the Vision 2025.
There has been a concerted effort among all parties to ensure that these exercises
inform and complement one another so that we can create program interventions that
are equally complementary.
Another important aim of the CCA and UNDAF exercises is to bring the unique strengths
of the United Nations to bear on the problems of Yemen in this new century. They
offer the possibility of increasing the relevance and reach of UN programming and of
including a wide range of development partners in the process. It is hoped that if
individual country programs can harness this experience and expertise through cooperative interventions that are more closely matched to national priorities and that
encourage UN agencies to work together toward common purposes, the UN globally will
increase its relevance and impact.
It is in this spirit that the UN and the Government of Yemen have undertaken the
UNDAF exercise. We realize that challenging ourselves to work collaboratively in
ways we have not previously worked poses some risks. But Yemen’s pressing development concerns require such action. The reduction of poverty, the promotion of human
development and human rights and the extension of democracy require us to work together and to use all available resources as efficiently and effectively as possible.
It also requires us to build alliances with civil society and international partners
— bilateral and multilateral donors and international NGOs. We welcome all of our
development partners to join us in this endeavor.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. In January 2001 the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) conducted a retreat to
discuss and finalize the Common Country Assessment (CCA) produced by interdisciplinary teams of their colleagues in Government, the UN and other development agencies. Several crosscutting themes were presented to the Minister
of Planning and Development (MOPD) and for further discussion and refinement.
As a result, three UNDAF themes were selected:
 Gender Equity with a Special Focus on Rural Areas
 Local Governance
 Enhancing Capacity for Policy Analysis and Program Development for
Human Development
2. A twelve-member UNDAF Steering Committee made up of representatives from the
Ministry of Planning and Development and senior UN staff began meeting weekly
immediately after the UNDAF retreat. The Committee worked collaboratively to
arrive at both the form and content of this document. The challenge was to
further define the objectives of the UNDAF and to formulate strategies and
activities that will encourage partnership and synergy both within the UN
system and among the UN, Government, and other development partners.
3. The UNDAF exercise was completed concurrently with a number of other planning
exercises, and the UN and the Government are making a concerted effort to
ensure that all of these documents and processes are mutually reinforcing.
The UN and the Government have already reaped benefits from their investment
in the CCA/UNDAF exercises in terms of increased communication and the sharing
of ideas and experiences.
4. Through its extensive discussions on the form and content of the UNDAF, the
UNDAF Steering Committee (see Annex 1 for a list of participants) came to a
consensus on three overarching principles to guide its work both on this
document and the UNDAF activities it describes. These principles are as
follows:
h A strong commitment to initiating activities that raise the public
profile of the UNDAF and increase understanding and appreciation for
its principles.
h Active encouragement and facilitation of the involvement of other domestic and international partners in the UNDAF.
h Realistic aims for UNDAF activities and interventions in its first
year.
5. It is important to note that the programming framework described in this
document does not represent the totality of the UN’s work in Yemen. The UNDAF
represents those crosscutting areas where the UN is committing its collective
talents and strengths to work in tandem with the Government as well as other
development partners.
6. In the period from unification in 1990 until today, Yemen has seen many
changes, some quite dramatic, in its human development situation. The population grew from 12.2 million to 18.7 million and the country registered an
increase of some 14 years in life expectancy at birth. Infant mortality and
under-five mortality rates declined by 15% and 31% respectively, and the
fertility rate declined from 7.8 live births to 6.5. On the political front,
Yemen has moved steadily toward national unity, increased political participation, and resolved border and sovereignty issues with its neighbors, most
recently the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.iv
7. Nevertheless, Yemen continues to be one of the least developed countries in
the world. While the Human Development Index (HDI)1 value increased from 0.242
to 0.448 in the last decade, the Global Human Development Report for the year
2000 ranks Yemen 148 among 174 countries in terms of the HDI.
8. Based on the theme papers that were developed as part of the CCA process, and
further consultations, discussions and constructive dialogue, the CCA identified the following key development challenges:
h Strengthening economic reforms.
h Ending food insecurity.
h Ensuring universal basic education, especially for girls.
h Improving public and reproductive health.
h Addressing the water crisis.
h Ensuring justice for all.
h Strengthening decentralization and promoting community participation.
h Enhancing national capacity for policy analysis, monitoring and evaluation.
9. There has been considerable sharing of resources and expertise among the
various national and UN planning exercises, resulting in a relatively consistent vision and approach among them. In terms of their main objectives and
specific themes, both the Vision 2025 and the Second Five-Year Plan concur in
general terms with the priorities set out in the CCA. The Vision 2025 cites
high population growth, water scarcity and governance and public administration as the main challenges facing the country.
10. The Five-Year Plan, while more focused on economic and good governance issues,
sets forth the following internal and external challenges:
Internal Challenges: Water scarcity, high population growth, aggravation of
unemployment, an inadequately trained human resource base, increasing poverty
levels, inadequate infrastructure, a weak enabling environment for investment
and undeveloped science and technology systems.
External Challenges: Preparing the Yemeni economy for globalization and integration with the world economy, the need for complementarity and economic
cooperation within the region and capitalizing on information technology.
11. In terms of measuring progress toward human development, both the CCA and
UNDAF rely upon the CCA Indicators. In addition, the UN will assist Yemen in
reporting on the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) endorsed by world leaders
at the UN Millennium Summit held in September 2000 and the indicator framework
of the Five-Year Plan. (See annexes 2, 3, and 4 for more detail on these
frameworks).
12. The analysis carried out as part of the CCA clearly stressed the underlying
importance and crosscutting nature of the themes. The UNDAF’s integrated and
complementary approach to these crosscutting themes is intended to support the
overarching goals of poverty eradication in tandem with improvement in human
development and human rights in the longer term. Moreover, in the case of a
number of suggested interventions, the UNDAF is recommending an area-based
approach. The Government will take the lead in suggesting those localities
where UNDAF collaboration would be most appropriate.
13. The UNDAF themes complement one another in many ways. Empowerment is idea
that unites all three of these themes. The UNDAF interventions seek to realize empowerment through a variety of means. Improvement in the three UNDAF
areas would have a crosscutting impact on basic development indicators, in1 A composite index based on three indicators: longevity, as measured by life expectancy
at birth; educational attainment, as measured by a combination of adult literacy (twothirds weight) and the combined gross primary, secondary, and tertiary enrolment ratio
(one-third weight); and standard of living, as measured by GDP per capita (PPP $US).v
cluding the Millennium Development Goals related to poverty reduction, health,
reproductive health, education and gender.
14. The implementation of UNDAF and joint or collaborative activities supported by
the UN system will have to be monitored closely. Success of the UNDAF will be
assessed not only on the basis of evaluations and/or assessments that measure
programmatic impact but also on the ability of the UN and the Government to
identify lessons learned and to make necessary corrections and adjustments in
their collaborative efforts.
15. The following management arrangements will be put in place and refined, as
necessary, during the UNDAF period:
Oversight Committee (OC): The oversight or review of the UNDAF will be carried out by a high level committee composed of the Minister of Planning and
Development, the UN Resident Coordinator, and the UNCT. Senior representatives from other Government entities, the donor community, and civil society
could participate depending on the nature of the UNDAF partnership arrangements. Whereas the primary function of the Oversight Committee will be to
review UNDAF implementation, it will also serve as a forum for the discussion
of other issues related to UN-Government collaboration or cooperation.
Thematic Operational Groups: Each Thematic Operational Group (TOG) will be cochaired by representatives from the Government and the UN. To ensure effectiveness and accountability, the UN team will be lead by a senior UN staff
person (supported by a “lead” UN agency) with significant professional expertise and experience in the area. The other members of each TOG will be senior
technical personnel from Government, UN-funded projects, donors and donorfunded projects, INGOs, NGOs and other interested representatives of civil
society (including academics and journalists) and the private sector.
In addition, a Coordination Unit composed of several senior officials from the
Ministry of Planning and Development (MOPD) and the UN will consolidate the
work of the TOGs for review and consideration by the Oversight Committee and
follow-up with the TOGs on the decisions taken by the Oversight Committee.
16. One of the most critical elements of the UNDAF exercise is partnership. Three
matrices that map out potential UNDAF partners according to each UNDAF theme
are presented in Annex 6. The actors listed are those who are potential
participants or resources to the TOGs. It is envisioned that the TOGs will
call upon these actors to participate in the Groups and ensure that any actions or interventions will complement, not duplicate, existing activities.
In addition, as noted in the description of the Oversight Committee, partners
with a strong presence or interest in a thematic area may serve on the Oversight Committee as deemed appropriate.
17.The UNDAF is a new endeavor for the Government, the UN, and their development
partners. It is meant to play a catalytic role in bringing partners together
and providing a mechanism for them to coordinate and share resources. It is
hoped that innovative and creative proposals will emerge for how to best
realize this new level of cooperation.1

theme areas is empowerment to promote and
protect human development and human
rights. Empowerment is vital to sustained
poverty eradication. All three themes
seek to create a more positive enabling
environment for sustainable development,
an important concept at this particular
time in Yemen. While development has
brought many benefits to Yemenis, including improvement in some of the basic
indicators of quality of life as well as
progress toward democracy, poverty has
increased over the last decade. Bringing
the benefits of development to the poor
and vulnerable will take concerted efforts to re-dress disparities and expand
participation. Progress in the three
thematic areas is expected to contribute

The UNDAF exercise was completed concurrently with a number of other planning
exercises and the UN and the Government
are making a concerted effort to ensure
that all of these documents and processes
are mutually reinforcing. The Cabinet
approved a National Population Strategy
in February 2001 and the Government is in
the process of finalizing a National
Action Plan for Poverty Eradication
(NAPPE). It is also preparing a Poverty
Reduction Strategy and Action Plan
(PRSAP), which the Boards of the World
Bank and IMF have introduced as one of
the prerequisites for access to
concessional financing. In addition, the
Second Five-Year Development Plan is
nearing completion, as is a longer-term
Vision 2025 document. A number of participants involved in the CCA/UNDAF
exercises are also active in these initiatives. It is hoped that this process
of “cross-fertilization” will help secure
a solid foundation for cooperation and
coordination between the Government, the
UN, and other development partners – a
much needed prerequisite for having a
positive and significant impact on the
state of human development in Yemen.
The CCA/UNDAF exercises represent a new
modus operandi for how the Government and
the UN realize cooperation among their
own agencies and offices as well as with
other development partners. Both the
institutions and the individuals involved
in the exercises to date have learned a
great deal about the commitments required
and gains to be realized from investing
in collaboration. The principle of collaboration is simple. However, in practice it requires a high degree of coordination and individual commitment. While
the idea of UN agencies working together
at the program/project level is not new,
to date such collaboration in Yemen has
been rather limited and ad hoc in nature.
The UN and the Government have already
reaped benefits from their investment in
the CCA/UNDAF exercises in terms of
increased communication and the sharing
of ideas and experiences. They have led
the UN and the Government to this joint
document and have shown a way forward on
many fronts that will aid all participants in putting the UNDAF into practice.
Key results and lessons learned from the
process include the following:
Ö A better understanding of Yemen’s
socio-economic situation as well as
the ways in which so many pressing
issues are both multi-sectoral and
interrelated.

Ö An appreciation for the challenge of
gathering and interpreting information
and statistics. Additionally, an
awareness that there is a need for
capacity and consensus building in the
area of statistics so that this valuable information can better aid policy
makers.
Ö A greater awareness and appreciation
for the expertise and experience of
local experts, who contribute in-depth
knowledge and unique insight.
Ö A realization that merely preparing
the UNDAF alone is insufficient.
Collaboration needs to be long-term
and continuous to yield measurable
results in terms of development indicators. In addition, collaboration
and the possibility of joint programming efforts require clear management
arrangements and a significant investment of time and resources.
Ö An appreciation of the importance of
linking government planning exercises
and other on-going processes in order
to reinforce collaboration, save time
and effort, and help mobilize resources to achieve shared targets.
Ö An emerging consensus on and acceptance of the human rights approach to
development among the international
and local development community that
will guide not only UNDAF but also all
future efforts to achieve progress on
crosscutting issues.

In the period from unification in 1990
until today, Yemen has seen many
changes, some quite dramatic, in its
human development situation. The population grew from 12.2 million to 18.7
million and the country registered an
increase of some 14 years in life expectancy at birth. Infant mortality and
under-five mortality rates declined by
15% and 31% respectively and the fertility rate declined from 7.8 live births to
6.5. On the political front, Yemen has
moved steadily toward national unity,
increased political participation, and
resolved border and sovereignty issues
with its neighbors, most recently the
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
Nevertheless, Yemen continues to be one
of the least developed countries in the
world. While the Human Development Index
(HDI) value increased from 0.242 to 0.448
in the last decade, the Global Human
Development Report for the year 2000
ranks Yemen 148 among 174 countries in
terms of the HDI. Poverty, illiteracy,
and malnutrition are widespread, and the
population is still growing rapidly. The
scarcity of water is reaching crisis
proportions. A large part of the population is unserved by modern infrastructure, and many inequalities stem from
rural-urban residence, gender, and membership in certain vulnerable groups.
The justice system is in need of capacity
building and reform, both to ensure
access for all citizens and to improve
the regulatory environment to attract
much needed investment for development.
The economy is vulnerable because it is
highly dependent on a single commodity,
oil, the price of which remains very
unstable.
The Five-Year Plan and the CCA emphasize
that poverty eradication will require
addressing persistent disparities and
differential access to basic social
services and development benefits. Many
citizens are still not full participants
or beneficiaries of the development
process. Based on theme papers that were
developed as part of the CCA process, and
further consultations, discussions and
constructive dialogue, the CCA identified
the following key development challenges:
Strengthening economic reforms: Despite
a stable macroeconomic situation, poverty
has increased in the last decade with an
estimated 34.9% of the population living
below the poverty line. Diversification
of the economy beyond the oil sector is
difficult due to three important factors:
low labor productivity, an inadequately
trained work force, and a weak regulatory
environment and judicial system that
inhibit much needed investment.
Ending food insecurity: Yemen is classified as a low-income and food deficit
(LIFDC) country and imports over 75% of
its main staple, wheat. While food
availability seems to be well secured
from imports, access is constrained by
low purchasing power. Extremely high
rates of malnutrition, low birth weight,
and infant mortality in many areas of
Yemen hint at serious chronic food access
shortfalls. Natural resource degradation
and depletion also pose a serious threat
to food security.
Ensuring universal basic education,
especially for girls: At present, 59% of
the school-age population is enrolled
with large disparities in gender, and
among governorates and rural and urban
locations. Economic factors as well as
deep-rooted social and cultural attitudes
and practices together with inadequate
provisioning of educational facilities
and the poor state of classrooms and
school buildings, account for low access
to education. The gross primary enrollment rate is the lowest in the Middle
East and North Africa region and far
below the Government’s basic education
enrolment target of 85% by 2000.
Improving public and reproductive health:
Currently, primary health care services
reach only 42% of the population with a
significant gap between urban and rural
areas (75% and 24% respectively). The
quality of services is low, especially in
the area of preventive health care.
Among children, diarrhoeal diseases and
acute respiratory infections are the
major causes of morbidity and mortality.
Furthermore, one-third of all deaths
among under-fives occur because of vaccine preventable diseases. The prevalence
of communicable diseases, including
malaria and tuberculosis, remain high.
In addition, maternal mortality and
morbidity are high because of limited
pre-, peri- and post-natal care, lack of
emergency obstetric care, early and
frequent pregnancies, and the low rate of
modern contraceptive use. Moreover, HIV/
AIDS is an area of concern.
Addressing the water crisis: Yemen is
located in one of the most water scarce
regions in the world. This situation is
II. YEMEN’S DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGES4
exacerbated by the great expansion of
groundwater pumping. The annual decline
of aquifer levels in most water basins
averages 1-8 meters. Current water
quantities pumped are estimated at 138%
(2.8 billion m3) of the annual renewal
capacity, estimated at around 2.1 billion
m3. This means that Yemen consumes 700
million m3 over and above its renewable
water resource causing water depletion.
Ensuring justice for all: Yemen has
stated its commitment to protecting and
promoting human rights. Nonetheless,
protection afforded by the justice sector
is constrained by many factors. With high
illiteracy rates, the geographic dispersion of the population and the absence of
awareness creation efforts, many citizens
remain unaware of their constitutional
and legal rights. Thus, they are unable
to exercise them. The complexity of
procedures, unawareness of the due process of law in courts and a perceived
lack of fairness lead many citizens to
seek out-of-court settlements for their
legal concerns.
Strengthening decentralization and promoting community participation: Recent
legislation and local elections underscore both government commitment in this
area as well as the tremendous amount of
planning, training, and awareness building that needs to take place for this
initiative to be successful in terms of
promoting democracy and strengthening the
effectiveness and efficiency of essential
public services. While informal social
networks abound in Yemen, especially
those based on tribal affiliation, rapid
urbanization has put traditional sources
of support and stability under a great
deal of stress, and they have yet to be
replaced by equitable and easily accessible government-sponsored social services.
Enhancing national capacity for policy
analysis, monitoring and evaluation: In
spite of the emphasis on economic reform
in the 1990s, there is wide recognition
of the need to strengthen government
capacity to implement programs, enforce
laws and provide more security. Public
administration suffers from poor institutional capabilities, inefficient personnel, under-paid and unmotivated civil
servants, inadequate training, and cumbersome procedures and management systems. In addition, there is a great need
for reliable and readily available statistics and other indicators to aid
policymakers in the process of setting
priorities and establishing sound public
policies to address the country’s most
pressing development concerns.5
As noted previously, a number of important national planning exercises are
well underway. There has been considerable sharing of resources and expertise
among these exercises, resulting in a
relatively consistent vision and approach
among the various instruments and exercises.

In terms of main objectives and specific
themes, both the Vision 2025 and the
Five-Year Plan concur in general terms
with the priorities set out in the CCA.
The Vision 2025 cites high population
growth, water scarcity and governance and
public administration as the main challenges facing the country. The Five-Year
Plan, while more focused on economic and
good governance issues, sets forth the
following internal and external challenges:
Internal Challenges: Water scarcity, high
population growth, aggravation of unemployment, an inadequately trained human
resource base, increasing poverty levels,
a weak enabling environment for investment, inadequate infrastructure, and
undeveloped science and technology systems.
External Challenges: Preparing the Yemeni
economy for globalization and integration
with the world economy, the need for
complementarity and economic cooperation
within the region, and capitalizing on
information technology.
The Five-Year Plan sets forth the following goals and objectives to achieve
economic growth, job opportunities and
the realization of economic and social
stability:
1. Achieving an average 6% growth rate in
the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and
an 8% growth rate in the non-oil GDP.
2. Increasing the contribution of the
goods sector by realizing average
growth rate between 8-15% that would
help diversify the economy.6
3. Motivating and encouraging domestic
and foreign private investments and
increasing the share of private investment in the overall total.
4. Increasing employment to absorb the
annual increase in the workforce and
to reduce unemployment to below 9%.
5. Curbing poverty and mitigating its
impact on the poor by means of cash
assistance on the one hand and creating jobs on the other so as to cut
back absolute poverty to less than 20%
by the end of the Plan.
6. Balancing budget revenues and spending
by the end of the Plan’s period.
7. Containing the inflation rate to
around 8% on average.
8. Establishing and activating a national
science and technology network to
facilitate information sharing and
encourage innovation.
9. Preparing the Yemeni economy to merge
into the world economy by means of
enhancing integration and cooperation
between Arab and regional partners in
order to maximize the advantages of
joining the World Trade Organization
(WTO).7
IV. YEMEN AND UN GOALS
There is general consensus among the
Government and its development partners on Yemen’s most pressing development
challenges. Central to all efforts will
be poverty eradication. The UN Charter
sets out three core interrelated goals:
peace, development, and human rights.
The UN Secretary-General’s reform proposals make human rights a crosscutting
theme for the entire UN system to be
achieved through efforts to increase
economic growth and through investing in
people – their health, education and
livelihoods. UN efforts encompass the
implementation of specific interventions
as well as monitoring assistance. Encouraged by the Government’s initiatives
to consolidate democracy and promote
greater participation, the UN aims to
play a proactive role in supporting and
advancing human development in a strategic way.
In terms of measuring progress toward
human development, both the CCA and UNDAF
rely upon the CCA Indicators. The framework for the CCA Indicators is provided
by the UN (see Annex 2 for a brief description). The primary purpose of these
indicators is to capture the many dimensions of poverty and to provide benchmarks for progress. Each indicator
refers to a UN conference or summit,
which has in many cases set specific
goals or targets. Thus, the CCA and
UNDAF provide a mechanism for measuring
progress toward a set of global UN targets emanating from UN conferences and
conventions attended by Yemen or to which
Yemen is a signatory. In addition, both
the CCA Core Indicators (30 total) and
the Non-Core Indicators (21 in the case
of Yemen’s CCA) were designed to be
compatible with the goals and indicators
endorsed by the Organization for Economic
Cooperation and Development (OECD).
Moreover, in September 2000 as a result
of the UN Millennium Summit, the Millennium Declaration was signed by 147 heads
of state and government. This declaration incorporates eight Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)4 and ten International Development Targets (IDTs) for the
year 2015 that are tied to UN-sponsored
world summits and global conferences.
(See Annex 3 for a description of the
MDGs, the IDTs and their respective
indicators).
The UN General Assembly requested the UN
Secretary General to report annually on
progress toward implementation of the
MDGs and to report more comprehensively
every five years. The Secretary-General
has announced his intention that these
reports serve to track progress and also
to support a dynamic campaign to help
keep these issues front and center on the
national and global agenda. UN Country
Teams around the world will work in
collaboration with government partners to
report on the MDGs as well as on local
capacity in the area of monitoring.
Yemen’s Ministry of Planning and Development has formulated its own indicator
framework to report on progress achieved
toward realization of the goals set forth
in its Five-Year Plan (Annex 4). Many of
these indicators correspond to the MDGs.
For the purpose of reporting and monitoring the UNDAF, there will be a concerted
effort to harmonize these various indicator frameworks in order to streamline
reporting and present progress toward
indicators in formats that are readily
understood and available to all development actors.
Another important goal of the UNDAF is to
work with partners in Government to use
these basic indicators to advocate strategically for assistance in those critical areas that are likely to have a
significant impact on poverty eradication
and human development. Based on data
received by the UN, the Official Development Assistance (ODA) disbursed for Yemen
in 2000 was US$ 298.0 million. Of this
amount, 53% came from multilateral donors
and 47% from bilateral donors. The UN
system contributed US$ 44.2 million (or
14.2%) of this total. Used strategically, it is hoped that UN assistance and
UNDAF interventions can act as a catalyst
for increasing the amount and the impact
of future ODA to Yemen.

The themes are envisioned as long-term in
nature. Much like the goals of the Vision
2025, the themes are broadly directional

agencies. It is hoped that this will
further reinforce collaborative efforts.

have been divided between time frames of
short-term (mid-2001 to mid-2002) and
medium to long term (five-year time

The analysis carried out as part of the
CCA clearly stressed the underlying
importance and crosscutting nature of the

complementary approach to these crosscutting themes is intended to support the
overarching goals of poverty eradication

longer term. Moreover, in the case of a
number of suggested interventions below,
the UNDAF is recommending an area-based
approach. It is hoped that such an

As delineated below, the UNDAF themes
complement one another in many ways.
Empowerment is the idea that unites all
three of these themes. The UNDAF interventions seek to realize empowerment
through a variety of means: improving
rural women’s access to and use of assets
and basic social services; strengthening
governance capacities at local levels
including citizens’ ability to exercise

identify their problems and needs and
formulate, implement, and monitor their

have a significant impact on Yemen’s
human development situation. Improvement

crosscutting impact on basic development
indicators, including the Millennium
Development Goals related to poverty

education and gender.

The theme of gender equity was selected
based on its potential to have farreaching affects on the human development
situation in Yemen and on the pressing
need to reduce gender disparities across
sectors. It was agreed that gender
equity as a whole would be too broad an
area to deal with holistically and that
it was necessary to narrow down the focus
to three or four key entry points that
would have broad based reverberations for
other aspects of the lives of women. It
was noted, for example, that improving
women’s access to and control over health
care would reduce maternal and infant
mortality as well as contribute to slower
population growth. Access to education
would, in turn, have a positive impact on
literacy, political participation and
labor productivity among women. Thus
this presentation concentrates on three
principle areas of intervention: basic
education, reproductive health and rights
and access to assets, all with a special
focus on rural women.
Despite the fact that Yemen has made
progress during the past three decades
towards gender equity, women’s participation in the development process and in
decision-making is very limited. Virtually all socio-economic indicators show
that women and girls remain comparatively
disadvantaged at national and sub-national levels, despite ongoing efforts to
mainstream gender concerns into national
policies and strategies. The situation
of women in rural areas is significantly
worse than in urban areas. Furthermore
the majority of Yemeni women remain ill
equipped to claim their basic rights such
as access to education and the labor
market. Women’s illiteracy stands at 64%.
The fourth World Conference on Women
(Beijing, 1995) and other UN conferences
have stated that there should be a universal obligation towards gender equality, development and peace. It was recognized that understanding women’s equality

B. Local Governance
Background and Rationale
In the analytical and consultative processes carried out under the CCA, the
deepening of people’s participation
emerged as a prerequisite for sustainable
human development. The CCA also highlighted the existence of many social
disparities in Yemen. Many citizens are
without access to basic social services
and are not full participants in or
beneficiaries of the development process.
Interventions in the area of local governance can have significant impact on
reducing disparities – in particular
disparities between rural and urban
populations, between men and women, and
in income. Indeed, one of the ways that
the success of decentralization can be
measured is by whether or not these
disparities are reduced.
The Government is committed to devolving
authority and a significant proportion of
resources to the local level in order to
be more responsive to the needs of communities. It is also committed to
strengthening the electoral process
especially in light of the local and
parliamentary elections to be held in
April 2003. Empowering local communities
and giving them a say in decisions governing their daily life should contribute
to reducing the confidence gap between
society and its government and thus help
establish a democratic sense of citizenship. In addition, it should facilitate
the mobilization of local resources in
the form of tax collection and voluntary
contributions that are expected to become
an important source for the investment of
local authorities in infrastructure and
services.
The process leading to the approval of
the Local Authority Law was marked by
intense debates and media coverage at
central and local levels. National ownership is clearly reflected by the fact
that the process was internally driven
and without any foreign involvement and
support. The Local Authority Law, passed
by Parliament and approved by Presidential Decree in February 2000, stipulates
that: “[…] the local authority law system
is based on the principle of administrative and financial decentralization, and
on the basis of expansion of popular
participation in decision making and
management of local concerns in the
sphere of economic, social and cultural
development.”5
Yemen will be aided in its decentralization efforts by a wealth of positive
traditions of self-government and civil
society participation. The tribal structure of the Yemeni society is underpinned
by a set values of solidarity and attachment to self-management that are likely
to have a positive impact on the initiative. Also, the experience of the Local
Development Associations (LDA) and the
cooperative system that prevailed in the
1970s and mid-1980s should be taken into
account in the context of this initiative. The proliferation of non-governmental organizations in the past few years
is another encouraging feature of the
dynamics of civil society in Yemen.
Within the purview of introducing a more
participatory approach to development,
the Government also recognizes the effectiveness of local governance as a means
of fostering equitable development and
mainstreaming human rights through
people’s participation, the promotion of
local ownership and a better valorization
of local human and material potential. In
a country where over 75 % of the population is rural, the implementation of
well-designed local governance initiatives is an effective tool for poverty
alleviation, the reduction of in-country
disparities and the promotion of economic
growth through the mobilization of private sector initiatives and community
energies.

most ambitious and challenging program
that the Government has undertaken since
the country’s unification. The successful
achievement of the overall political,

mistrust and indifference towards state
authority dictate that UN support to
local governance and community participation be articulated around a set of
strategies that take into account the
specific conditions of Yemen and the
overall requirements of the reform program. The structure of society, the
dispersion of the population, in-country
disparities, high illiteracy rates, weak
infrastructure, an alarming lack of
capacities (organizational, managerial,
financial) and an inadequate understanding of decentralization are indicative of
the magnitude of the challenges and risks
ahead.
The strategies selected for UN support to
these areas are based on knowledge of the
country and experience accumulated during
more than 40 years of development cooperation in the country as well as experiences with decentralization in other
developing countries. The analysis carried out as part of the preparation
process for the CCA and the assessments
made by a joint World Bank, UNCDF and
UNDP mission in 2000 have already provided useful insights into the magnitude
of the problems and issues to be addressed. Downstream activities covering
the four strategies below are envisaged,
with local governments and civil society
groups undertaking concrete development
activities.
Policy dialogue: The UN will use its
comparative advantage to expand and
deepen the dialogue among all stakeholders and to promote a better understanding among policy makers of the
various decentralization policy options and their broad implications.
This entails interaction with all the
forces that are likely to impact the
program at central, regional and
district levels. Particularly important in this context is the involvement of civil society and the private
sector, Interventions at different
levels are likely to have mutually
reinforcing impacts and to improve
recognition of the value of cooperation and dialogue.17
Capacity Development: Public administration suffers from poor institutional capacities, insufficient personnel, under-paid and poorly motivated civil servants, inadequate
training and cumbersome procedures and
management systems. Furthermore, great
variations are found between districts
and governorates in terms of resource
endowment, economic activities, and
administrative capacities, which call
for the design of programs based on
careful situation analyses and assessments. UN support in this area will
shift from the narrow focus of training to encompass capacity building in
its broader sense. It will address as
a priority, decision-making, management and organizational systems as
well as human resource development.
Although there has been no direct UN
support to decentralization, a number
of UN-supported projects in other
thematic areas had a decentralization
component, which could be built upon
and consolidated.
Advocacy: The implementation of decentralization requires strong, locally
based constituencies to support these
efforts. Assistance to local authorities, elected councils, and traditional leaders will enhance the sense
of ownership and enhance their role as
facilitators for the mobilization of
communities. In addition, the mobilization of civil society organizations
through awareness and partnershipbuilding is an important element of
success in any decentralizationrelated initiative. In a country known
for its heavily centralized governance
system, there may be a tendency to
focus on administrative
deconcentration or a reluctance to
devolve decision making powers to
local bodies. Therefore, continuous
advocacy efforts are required not only
to change attitudes but also to establish effective collaborative arrangements between stakeholders.
Empowerment: Support to local capacities is an essential instrument for
solving local problems. Empowerment
of communities, not only in terms of
providing much needed material and
financial resources but also by expanding basic knowledge and understanding of their rights, roles and
responsibilities, will be one the
cornerstones of the UNDAF strategy in
this area. Awareness and capacity
building initiatives combined with job
and income-generating activities at
the community level constitute strong
incentives for the mobilization of
communities. Women, as the most dynamic factor in rural areas, will be
targeted as a priority. NGOs can also
be important partners in complementing
the role of public institutions.
Projects and programs related to
poverty reduction efforts, gender
equity, education and health would
form the tangible instruments through
which communities can be empowered.
It is envisioned that area-based approaches will be pursued to facilitate
the design of integrated, efficient and
high impact programmes of support and to
ensure synergies between the three objectives of the UNDAF.
Short Term Actions
Because of the long-term nature of decentralization programs, their complexity
and the lack of capacities, the initial
phase of implementation of the program is
likely to be difficult and perhaps even
frustrating. Therefore, the basic foundation of the UN system support will be to
assist the government in the articulation
of a long term framework for decentralization. The first pillar of the program
is the development among practitioners of
a broad understanding of what decentralization means, its different forms, how it
can be planned and implemented and how
its challenges can be overcome. Dialogue
with national authorities will focus on
the nature, depth and characteristics of
the decentralization programme. It will
touch upon issues such as the functional
relationships between central and local
bodies, legislation, planning, and financial autonomy and accountability systems.
This will be followed by a thorough
assessment of needs and requirements and
the setting up of priority intervention
areas at central, intermediate and local
levels. This will help design an overall
strategic framework for long and medium
term interventions by the UN system and
other development partners.
The design of such a framework will be
based on the following complementary,
high impact actions:
 A thorough analysis of capacities
requirements and a national conference
on governance.
 A review of the various communitybased and area-based approaches in
terms of community mobilization.
 A workshop for governors.18
 Training activities for a select
number of local councils, local governmental and non-governmental institutions.
 An awareness raising campaign using a
multimedia approach that targets all
partners central and local government
institutions and communities.
 A workshop for training of trainers.
 Design of a Technical Cooperation
among Developing Countries (TCDC)
arrangement for interaction and exchanges with other developing countries that have gone through decentralization processes.
Medium and Long Term Actions
Decentralization is by definition a very
long term, transformational process that
requires flexibility, constant refinement
of approaches and systematic follow up
and monitoring. In fact, the Government
may opt to retain some functions and
powers and adopt a phased approach in the
implementation of the Local Authority
Law. The UN system will access international experience and knowledge in order
to avoid the typical problems associated
with the implementation of local governance programs. The lessons learned from
short-term actions (phase I) will be
articulated into a multi year program,
which will consolidate and refine
achievements and extend assistance to
other areas (districts and governorates).
Capacity development
 Work with a select number of central
ministerial departments that are
willing to devolve some of their
functions to local governments. This
should cover the elaboration and
development of tools and instruments
(human resource management, service
delivery, information systems, budgeting, policy and legislation,
etc.).
 Pilot interventions in selected
governorates and districts to address problems at the sub-national
level and to test methods that could
be subsequently applied throughout
the country. Programmes in this area
could include the establishment of
organizational structures and capacities for participatory planning
at district and local levels that
involve stakeholders and local administrators.
 Support to local communities in poor
districts for the development of
innovative rural development
schemes, non-farm employment, smallscale, labor-intensive activities,
community priority-setting, project
implementation and follow up. With
empowerment combined with awareness
and civic education, people will
become more pre-occupied with the
quality of their environment and are
expected to display a stronger commitment to contribute to the management of their natural resources.
 Provide Information systems at the
district level in particular to
serve as the basis for regional
planning, implementation of local
development initiatives and establishment of appropriate monitoring
and evaluation systems.
Partnerships
In light of the magnitude of the challenges ahead that are beyond the means of
any single donor, it is essential that a
critical mass of support be provided to
have lasting impact. The Yemeni political
and economic reform program in general
and decentralization in particular, are
attracting attention from the international community. The UN system will
involve the widest possible range of
partners to work on different fronts
toward the overarching objective of
poverty eradication and the promotion of
peoples’ participation. This will entail
the design of mechanisms for sustainable
partnerships with both traditional and
non-traditional donors. The Bretton Woods
institutions, the private sector and NGOs
will be called upon to contribute to the
design and implementation of programs as
well as to their monitoring and evaluation. Needless to say that the Ministry
of Planning and Development and the
Ministry of Local Authority will be key
partners with whom close collaboration
links will be put in place.19
C. Enhancing Capacity for Policy Analysis and
Programme Development for Human Development
Background and Rationale
The selection and articulation of this
UNDAF objective came about not only due
to its emergence as a crosscutting development challenge but also as a direct
result of the CCA process. In the course
of information gathering and analysis for
the CCA as well as the UNDAF preparation,
it became increasingly apparent that the
links between information, analysis,
dissemination and policy making need to
be strengthened. Efforts to strengthen
informational infrastructure and data
gathering have not fully taken into
consideration the needs of Government
policymakers, NGOs, citizens and other
development partners for reliable and
readily available data in order to play
their respective roles in Yemen’s development process.
A specific focus on these actors and
their needs in the policy process would
reinforce efforts at decentralization,
democratization and participation in
addition to improving data quality for
all development efforts, across all
sectors of the economy and society.
Recent surveys and reports suggest that
the planning and implementation of development policies and programs in Yemen
still lacks a solid information support
system. While considerable progress has
been made in the past decade towards the
strengthening of national statistical
capacities, there remain serious gaps and
inconsistencies in the quality of data,
as well as in their dissemination and
use.
Despite the existence of adequate mechanisms at the central level for the monitoring of macro-economic indicators and
for ex-post financial auditing, the
operational capacity to evaluate the
outcomes and impacts of development
programs is weak. Similarly there is a
lack of gender-disaggregated data. In
addition, little advantage has been taken
of the latest technological advances to
accelerate the analysis and dissemination
of information as well as to maintain
databases.
The mandate of the UN includes supporting
national efforts to monitor the implementation of the resolutions of UN summits
and conferences, as well as the development goals and targets agreed to at the
recent UN Millennium Summit. Within the
broad area of data management, the UN
will provide support at national and subnational levels to improve and streamline
data gathering, analysis and dissemination, and the use of information for
development planning, monitoring and
evaluation. This will entail the setting
up of methodologies and standards and a
core set of indicators covering a wide
range of areas such as poverty reduction,
gender mainstreaming, reproductive
health, in-country disparities, child
labour, etc. Also, the possibility of
harnessing appropriate information technology in these processes will form an
integral part of the UN’s assistance.
Objectives
Theme: The national and
subnational data management capacity to: collect quality data
related to human development
(including human rights and natural resources); disaggregate data
by gender and community; analyze
and use data in development planning, and disseminate development
information to all actors in the
decision making process are improved.
The objectives of the UNDAF in
this area are to:
 Enhance national and subnational capacities for planning, monitoring and evaluating policies and programs
designed to improve human
development and human rights
in Yemen.
 Strengthen the statistical
capacity of all pertinent
organizations at the central,
sectoral and local governorate
levels to expand the availability, access and use of
quality gender sensitive data.
 Bridge statistical information
gaps wherever they exist.20
Strategies
Capacity building: With the introduction
of new economic and development concepts
there is need for a review of practices
and the setting up of quality standards
and procedures. The adoption of uniform
methodologies will improve data reliability, integrity and consistency, as well
as facilitate in-country and regional and
international comparisons. Bearing in
mind that with the implementation of the
decentralization program a number of
development related functions will be
undertaken at the local level, support to
a select number of districts and governorates (as a pilot operation) will be
required in the area of program and
project design, development, and monitoring and evaluation. This will also enhance synergy with the other UNDAF themes
of gender equity and local governance.
In this context, the UNDAF will seek to
strengthen institutions engaged in data
production, analysis and dissemination by
strengthening the national statistical
system at central (including academic and
research institutions) and local levels.
For instance, training will be provided
to statistics staff on how to integrate
gender analysis for future census and
surveys. Further, interventions will
support capacity building in applying
social assessments to bridge data gaps
and through the application of alternative and non-traditional assessment
techniques. This will allow policy
makers to obtain operationally relevant
social information for program design,
implementation and monitoring. It is
hoped that such information will assist
in the development of cost-effective,
decentralized programs. Finally, the
UNDAF will also offer opportunities for
access to best international practices
and facilitate the introduction of results-based approaches to better evaluate
progress towards the achievement of set
targets.
Advocacy: UNDAF implementation will
require the UN to strengthen its advocacy
with government on the importance of data
for policies and programs that are crucial in promoting human development and
human rights. Creating awareness among
policy makers at all levels on the use of
gender-sensitive data to facilitate
program development and monitoring will
constitute an important element in
achieving the sustainability of a data
and information system. Furthermore, the
dissemination of core CCA indicators and
Millennium Development Goals and targets
will constitute an instrument for empowering civil society. Similarly, social
assessments consistent with a rightsbased approach would be especially useful
in making the poor aware of their rights.
Networking: Developing a common set of
indicators and applying standard procedures, methodologies and access to reliable, quality data requires a crosssectoral and coordinated approach. The
Government and the UN will therefore work
closely with other stakeholders to ensure
coordination and common approaches.
Adequate attention will be given to avoid
overburdening already scarce national
capacities. Surveys should only be conducted to the extent that they relate to
key national priorities and to the measurement of progress towards achieving
the targets set as a follow up of international conferences.
UN support will build upon the achievements made so far in strengthening the
national statistical system. The recently
completed Poverty Information Monitoring
System (PIMS), the Labour Market Information System (LMIS), and other recent
exercises such as the Demographic Health
Survey (DHS) and the on-going agricultural census supported by the European
Commission constitute valuable assets.
Likewise, data compiled for Yemen’s first
National Human Development Report (NHDR,
1998) and the data being assembled and
the network established for the second
NHDR that is under preparation, are other
important assets. Efforts will also be
made to establish operational links
between ongoing and future UN-supported
projects, surveys and studies.
Short Term Actions
 A stocktaking exercise will be undertaken to define problem areas and the
exact nature and coverage of UN support.
 Completion and refinement of the 20/20
Basic Social Services initiative
(ongoing with United Nations
Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and UNDP
support). The results of the study
will enable national authorities and
the donor community to better target
development programs.
 Finalization of the CCA database and
setting up of a sustainable mechanism
for its maintenance and updating.
Moreover, as a follow-up to the Millennium Summit, a core set of indicators will be monitored to track
progress towards the realization of
Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)21
and their corresponding targets (see
Annex 3 for further detail on these
goals and targets).
 Advocacy activities such as workshops
and other training events to create
consensus on core development indicators.
 Strengthening of monitoring and evaluation capabilities and the involvement
of a larger number of stakeholders
(academic and audit institutions, line
ministries, Parliament, etc). This
might entail setting up a forum for
dialogue with concerned institutions
under the leadership of the Ministry
of Planning and Development in order
to define needs and requirements and
to plan for medium and long term UN
assistance.
Medium and Long Term Actions
The importance of information sharing and
performance evaluation needs to be seen
in the broader context of good governance. However, international experience
suggests that strengthening national
statistical systems and developing evaluation capabilities are long and difficult
processes. Therefore, based on the
achievements already made, and given the
multiplicity of stakeholders, UN support
will initially concentrate on the following:
 The establishment of a strong oversight mechanism, including enhancement
of staff skills and introduction of
modern tools (e.g. efficiency, impact
and sustainability analyses) to assist
the MOPD in assuming the important
responsibilities of continuously
monitoring and evaluating the implementation of key national development
strategies. The possibility of a
twinning arrangement with foreign
institutions with a similar mandate
will be explored.
 The launching of a human rights program in Yemen supported by the Office
of the High Commissioner for Human
Rights (OHCHR), UNDP and the World
Health Organization (WHO) offers a
unique opportunity to incorporate the
human rights dimension into this
programme.
 Support to the Food Insecurity, Vulnerability, Information and Mapping
System (FIVIMS) and the Early Warning
System launched by Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
 Promotion of national evaluator networks.
 Introduction of appropriate technologies.
Partnerships
For many years the UN system and other
donors provided significant support in
various forms to the national statistical
system, particularly to the Central
Statistical Organization (CSO). In
addition, support was also provided in
data collection and information systems
in line ministries (Planning, Public
Health, and Agriculture). Direct support projects were often related to the
specific concerns of the donors. Although
these projects have generated a lot of
data, in Yemen as in other developing
countries, they have overburdened national capacities and produced overlaps
and duplications. Therefore, the setting
up of a strong coordination mechanism led
by national authorities is vital so as to
achieve consistency and maximize the use
of both national and external resources.
In addition, the improvement of the
national information system is bound to
have a positive impact on advocacy,
resource mobilization and aid coordination in Yemen. It may also contribute
significantly to the organization of a
roundtable mechanism to attract additional international support for the
implementation of Yemen’s poverty reduction strategies, including those set
forth in the Poverty Reduction Strategy
and Action Plan (PRSAP) that is currently
under preparation.2223
A. Management Arrangements
In order to move forward with the implementation of the UNDAF, management arrangements need to be delineated at both
the thematic or substantive levels for
each of the UNDAF areas as well at the
oversight level for the UNDAF as a whole.
The implementation of UNDAF and joint or
collaborative activities supported by the
UN system will have to be monitored
closely. Success of the UNDAF will be
assessed not only on the basis of evaluations and/or assessments that measure
programmatic impact but also on the
ability of the UN and the Government to
identify lessons learned and to make
necessary corrections and adjustments in
their collaborative efforts.
The management arrangements for the UNDAF
consist of two key dimensions:
¨ Oversight Committee
¨ Thematic Operational Groups
Oversight Committee:
The oversight or review of the UNDAF will
be carried out by a high level committee
composed of the Minister of Planning and
Development (MOPD), the UN Resident
Coordinator and the UN Country Team
(UNCT) in Yemen. Senior representatives
from other Government entities, the donor
community and civil society could participate depending on the nature of the
UNDAF partnership arrangements. Whereas
the primary function of the Oversight
Committee will be to review UNDAF implementation, it will also serve as a forum
for discussion of other issues related to
UN-Government collaboration.
The main functions of the UNDAF Oversight
Committee will be to:
¨ Review the annual work plan and
progress reports of the Thematic
Operational Groups (TOGs).
¨ Discuss emerging national and
international policies, plans and
developments of relevance to the
UNDAF.
¨ Propose key upstream/policy areas
where joint UN support is likely
to have a significant impact on
eradicating poverty.
¨ Propose mechanisms for synergies,
complementarities and integration
between national programmes, UN
supported programs and activities
of other development partners.
¨ Advise on ways and means of addressing constraints and difficulties encountered in the implementation of UNDAF activities.
¨ Contribute to certain UNDAF activities, especially as they relate to advocacy and policy issues.
The OC will meet once or twice a year,
depending on the agenda proposed.
In addition, a joint MOPD-UNCT Coordination Unit will be set up to assist the
MOPD and the UNCT to fulfill their UNDAF
oversight responsibilities. The Unit
will consolidate the work of the various
TOGs for review and consideration by the
Oversight Committee. It will also follow-up with the TOGs on the decisions
taken by the Oversight Committee and
perform other UNDAF-related duties as
needed.
Thematic Operational Groups (TOGs):
The objectives, strategies and activities
(short and long term) outlined in the
UNDAF will be taken into consideration in
the design, formulation and implementation of various UN programming documents.
The Thematic Operational Groups (TOGs)
will form the concrete instruments for
translating UNDAF plans into reality and
for identifying and monitoring joint
collaborative activities. Existing UN
operational groups such as those in the
areas of HIV/AIDS and information will be
maintained.
The main functions of the UNDAF TOGs will
be to:
¨ Keep abreast of national policies
and plans in their respective
areas.
¨ Draw and maintain an inventory of
Government, UN system and non-UN
system activities and plans in
their respective thematic areas.
¨ Identify and propose opportunities
for collaborative activities.
¨ Self-manage its own operations
through generating meeting agendas, minutes, information sharing,
follow-up actions and reporting.
¨ Draft annual work plans with midyear updates for submission to the
UNCT for discussion at the Oversight Committee.

As previously underscored, one of the
most critical elements of the UNDAF

C. Monitoring and Evaluation
In order to reduce the reporting burden
on all actors, the UNDAF will rely on
existing reporting mechanisms wherever
and whenever possible. There are a
number of existing UN reports which will
provide natural entry points for UNDAF
review. These may include the following:
The Annual Report of the Resident Coordinator This report includes progress
achieved in UN system collaboration
overall and on UNDAF objectives specifically. It also presents a work plan for
all Resident Coordinator (RC)-related
activities, including the UNDAF.
Periodic Updating of the CCA Indicator
Framework This work will be carried out
by Government with the initial support of
the joint MOPD-UNCT Coordination Committee. The updated indicators can then be
shared with all TOGs for their reporting
requirements.
Annual Report on the Five-Year Plan This

Planning and Development, will contain
information on progress toward basic
indicators as well as progress reports on

Poverty Information Monitoring System and

will provide information and statistics

National Millennium Development Goal

THE UNDAF PROCESSYemen: The UNDAF Process
In Yemen, the CCA/UNDAF process, which ultimately involved the 
talents and insights of close to 100 participants, began 
formally in May 2000, when through a workshop inaugurated by 
the Minister of Planning and Development, UN agencies came to 
a common understanding on the purpose, scope and components of 
the exercise. 
In October, CCA "theme teams" were convened with the purpose 
of allowing for broad based consultation and consensus 
building. These teams, which went through a formal process of 
team building, were composed of UN agency heads and project 
staff, technical personnel from the Government, NGO 
representatives, academicians, subject experts and other 
development actors. Each theme team developed a paper on a 
critical area of concern under the guidance and authorship of 
a designated team leader. The papers were completed and 
reviewed collectively in November. Based on these papers, a 
draft CCA document was prepared and circulated to a wide 
audience in December 2000. This document provided the 
starting point for the UNDAF exercise.
At the UNDAF retreat conducted in January 2001 detailed 
comments on the CCA were invited from participants, who 
included the UN agency representatives and members of the 
CCA/UNDAF Steering Committee. Through intensive deliberations 
based on issues and priorities identified in the CCA, focus 
areas for UN system cooperation were discussed. Eight areas 
were identified as being of critical significance:
• Strengthening economic reforms.
• Ending food insecurity.
• Ensuring universal basic education especially for 
girls.
• Improving public and reproductive health.
• Addressing the water crisis. 
• Ensuring justice for all.
• Strengthening decentralization and community 
participation.
• Enhancing national capacity for policy analysis, 
monitoring and evaluation.
The focus for future UN collective attention was further 
narrowed by identifying three crosscutting themes. Broad 
strategies for resource allocation and mobilization, planning, 
implementation, monitoring and review were also discussed. 
These themes were then discussed with the Minister of Planning 
and Development and his associates and consensus was achieved. 
Immediately after the UNDAF Retreat, a joint UN-Government 
Steering Committee began its work. (The members of this 
Steering Committee are listed at the end of this annex). 
Through regular meetings over the course of four months, the 
Committee, in regular contact and consultation with the UNCT and colleagues in Government, produced this document. At key 
stages, drafts of the document were sent to outside readers 
for comments. These readers included local partners, the 
United Nations Development Group Office (UNDGO), and UN 
Agencies, Funds and Programmes. In all, the Committee 
received over 50 detailed comments and suggestions, many of 
which were incorporated.
 
In June 2001, the Steering Committee and the UNCT discussed a 
final draft of the UNDAF with His Excellency Ahmed Sofan of 
the Ministry of Planning and Development for consideration and 
approval. Subsequently, the UNDAF was circulated to 
Government ministries and development partners in Yemen and 
abroad. An UNDAF launch workshop is planned for September 
2001.

facilitate follow-up by national policymakers on progress in achieving them. To a large

Analysis
As of June 2001, the UNDG has begun to develop guidelines for reporting on 
Millennium Goals that take into consideration the following principles: 
• The reports should build on existing mechanisms and instruments, especially 
national development planning processes, PRSP, CCA and UNDAF to minimize 
the burden on Government, UN Country Teams and partners.• The reports should aim to build national ownership and capacity for tracking, 
monitoring and highlighting policy issues.
• The recognition that country reports need to reflect the MDGs in the country 
specific context, and that no size fits all. 
In order to facilitate analysis, UN Development Group has suggested an analytical 
framework for assessing the progress toward each target. It is envisioned that a report 
on progress toward each target might be structured as follows:
1. What is the trend for the 1990s that lies behind these figures? 
(e.g. steady improvement, slow improvement, uneven progress? Stability? Steady
or uneven worsening?) (2-3 lines)
2. Is the country on track for this 2015 target? 
(Yes, because....No, because....Make an assessment for the overall country-wide 
performance, but it would also be useful to comment here on the patterns – if
known – with regard to gender, geographic, income, ethnic & other inequalities
(1-2 paragraphs)
3. What are the major factors which will contribute to success or failure in 
meeting the target? What policies is the Government following which could 
help?
4. What would be needed from the country’s development partners?
(Any comments here are bound to be somewhat speculative, but it would be useful 
to state, where applicable what kinds of technical cooperation or other aid efforts
would help) (1 paragraph)
5. What is being done by the UN system in support?
